notes: Sweden gets Gothenburg, Malmö and Haparanda (#206). Gothenburg sits between Oslo and Copenhagen with its own exchange, Malmö faces Copenhagen across the Øresund, and Haparanda on the Finnish border is where the fibre crosses over land to Finland, with no exchange yet for you to found one. A Nordic fibre carrier sells transit along that route from Berlin to the border, and Swedish home networks reach the new cities.

The NOC charts have tooltips, on the dashboard and on the wallboard in the NOC window: hover (or touch) a chart to see every series on that day, with a total. Click an entry in the legend to hide or show that series, and the scale follows what is left. The "how it arrives" bars on the Traffic tab show the same kind of tooltip, and its legend picks which ways in (caches, PNIs, IX peering, transit) the table counts.

Bilbao joins the map, where the transatlantic cables really come ashore: Marea Carey, Grace Hopscotch and Sol Survivor now land there instead of Madrid. It has no exchange of its own, so traffic heads inland to Madrid, and Drizzle Electric, Tangerine Telecom and the big carriers sell transit there. A link you already run on the old Madrid landings keeps working as a plain subsea link, and the Mid-Atlantic Accent scenario now goes Azores, Bilbao, Madrid, and Marea Carey now leaves the American coast at Virginia Beach instead of crossing the northeast to New Jersey. Columbus III-and-a-half now comes ashore near Cádiz, where it really landed, on its way to Madrid.

Puzzles are easier to read, above all on phones: the three stars are now three goals in plain words, and the one you are working on says what is wrong and what to do, with a Show me button. The map marks it too: a red ring around a city that still needs traffic, and a pulsing ✂ on a link whose cut would hurt. On phones the sheet starts small so the map gets the screen; swipe it up for the rest. Cities far from the puzzle are left off the map, and stepping stones you are not using are small dots without a name until you tap one, build there or zoom in.

The map is now drawn by the graphics card wherever the browser can, so panning, zooming and fast play stay smooth on big networks and big screens. The map looks the same, and zoomed out the card draws the coastlines with fewer points where the extra detail was smaller than a pixel, which helps phones most. Settings › Map drawing › Always 2D keeps the old drawing and frees what the graphics card held, and browsers without WebGL2 or without a usable graphics card keep it on their own. If the graphics card stops for a moment (on a phone, switching apps can do that), the map is drawn in 2D until it is back, and stays in 2D for a game where it keeps failing. (#281)
Cities, labels, building cones, ships, offer bubbles and money pop-ups are painted once and then reused, so the map also draws far fewer shapes each frame. (#281)

In Firefox on a computer, the 2D map is up to three times as fast when zoomed in: its land picture now stays on the graphics card instead of being sent to it again on every frame. Firefox on Android keeps the old way, which avoids its drawing glitches. (#281)

Settings › Viewport info is now Diagnostic info: besides your screen's size, it shows how the map is drawn (by the graphics card or in 2D, and why) and how fast, ready to copy into a bug report. (#281)

Clean traffic that a scrubbing center sends back to a customer under attack no longer shows as DDoS junk on your backbone links; a link now lists it as scrubbed clean traffic, so a small flood no longer looks like hundreds of gigabits of junk (#289).

Alien waves you rent out on your dark fiber are now priced against the fiber itself: a wave costs a share of what leasing and lighting that fiber would cost the buyer, and each wave sold between the same two cities goes a little cheaper than the last. A route sold out to its market now earns a few times its lease, not dozens, and contracts already signed keep their price (#203).
Extra crews can now cut a fiber build on land to half its planned time at most, since permits and rights of way do not speed up; the button shows the day it would be done (#203).
A link ordered by typing both ends (the AI tools) can no longer end in a city the map does not show (#203).
